catalogue.title: Full-disk encryption not enabled
detect: Walk parents of the device mounted at /; pass if any ancestor has TYPE == "crypt"
catalogue.fix: Explain options: reinstall with encryption (safest), or offline in-place conversion with "cryptsetup reencrypt --encrypt" (risky, requires full backup). Never automate.
catalogue.why: Anyone who takes the device or boots a live USB can read every file. Most other at-rest checks become far more serious when this fails.

catalogue.title: Some mounted filesystems are not encrypted
detect: For every mounted block filesystem except /boot and /boot/efi, require a crypt ancestor
catalogue.fix: Recommend encrypting the affected volume (LUKS) after backing it up.
catalogue.why: Root is encrypted but /home, a second drive, or a data partition is not, so the user's files may sit in plain text while the system appears protected.

catalogue.title: Swap on an unencrypted device or filesystem
detect: TYPE partition: require crypt ancestor in lsblk
TYPE file: resolve backing block device (findmnt -T <file>) and require crypt ancestor
zram devices pass (see enc.swap_persistent for writeback)
catalogue.fix: Move swap onto LUKS, or replace with zram (zram-generator). Warn that ephemeral swap disables hibernation.
catalogue.why: Decrypted data from encrypted volumes (documents, passwords, keys) is paged out in plain text.

catalogue.title: Hibernation image written to unencrypted storage
detect: Check the resume device (and resume_offset swap file) has a crypt ancestor
catalogue.fix: Put swap on LUKS or disable hibernation.
catalogue.why: The hibernation image is a copy of all RAM, including LUKS master keys for other volumes, open documents and unlocked password manager contents.

catalogue.title: Swap keeps old memory on the disk across restarts
detect: If swap is zram: check /sys/block/zram*/backing_dev; anything other than "none" means writeback to disk
If swap is LUKS: check /etc/crypttab for a random key (/dev/urandom) vs a persistent keyslot
Note: zswap (/sys/module/zswap/parameters/enabled) still writes to disk swap; it is not zram
catalogue.fix: Offer zram-generator, or crypttab swap with a random key. Warn that both rule out hibernation.
catalogue.why: Old swapped-out data stays recoverable by anyone who later gets the LUKS passphrase (for example through compelled disclosure).

catalogue.title: Disk encryption passphrase is easier to brute-force than it needs to be (LUKS key slots)
detect: Flag "Version: 1" or any keyslot with "PBKDF: pbkdf2"
catalogue.fix: Explain "cryptsetup luksConvertKey --pbkdf argon2id". Warn that GRUB-decrypted /boot may not support Argon2id and the machine could become unbootable.
catalogue.why: LUKS1 and PBKDF2 keyslots are much cheaper to brute-force than Argon2id. Common on installs that encrypt /boot for GRUB.

catalogue.title: TPM-only disk unlock without a PIN
detect: cryptsetup luksDump <device>: systemd-tpm2 token with "tpm2-pin: false"
catalogue.fix: systemd-cryptenroll --wipe-slot=tpm2 --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-with-pin=yes <device>
catalogue.why: The disk unlocks automatically at boot, so protection depends entirely on the login screen. Combined with autologin, nothing protects the data.

catalogue.title: Backups are not encrypted
detect: Déjà Dup: gsettings list-recursively org.gnome.DejaDup; check repository for encryption
Duplicity: volumes ending in .gpg are encrypted
Borg: borg info <repo> shows Encrypted; restic always encrypts
catalogue.fix: Recommend an encrypting tool (restic, borg, Déjà Dup with encryption) or a LUKS target drive.
catalogue.why: Backups often outlive the original data and are stored on easily lost drives.

catalogue.title: External or removable drives are not encrypted
detect: lsblk -J -o NAME,FSTYPE,RM,HOTPLUG,MOUNTPOINTS; flag RM/HOTPLUG devices without crypto_LUKS
catalogue.fix: Offer guidance to format new drives with LUKS (GNOME Disks / KDE Partition Manager).

catalogue.title: Core dumps and crash reports kept on disk
catalogue.fix: Drop-in coredump.conf.d with Storage=none and ProcessSizeMax=0; delete existing dumps; disable apport.
catalogue.why: Dumps contain process memory from browsers, password managers and messengers.

catalogue.title: Filesystem snapshots keep deleted files
catalogue.fix: Explain that deleted files persist until snapshots expire; suggest excluding sensitive subvolumes and shorter retention.

catalogue.title: System journal kept indefinitely
catalogue.fix: Drop-in journald.conf.d with MaxRetentionSec=2week (or Storage=volatile); journalctl --vacuum-time=2weeks.
catalogue.why: Records USB serials, Wi-Fi SSIDs, volume labels, sudo command lines and app messages.

catalogue.title: Trash not emptied (including on removable drives)
detect: GNOME: gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.privacy remove-old-trash-files / old-files-age
catalogue.fix: Empty on confirmation; enable automatic removal of old trash on GNOME.

catalogue.title: Unencrypted /boot without Secure Boot (evil-maid risk)
catalogue.fix: Explain Secure Boot and measured boot options. Note the kernel lockdown mode (/sys/kernel/security/lockdown): confidentiality stops even root reading kernel memory.
catalogue.why: An attacker with brief physical access can modify the initramfs to capture the disk passphrase.

catalogue.title: /tmp is on disk rather than in memory
catalogue.fix: Enable tmp.mount (systemd) or an fstab tmpfs entry.

catalogue.title: TRIM passed through LUKS
detect: grep discard /etc/crypttab; cryptsetup status <name> shows "flags: discards"
catalogue.fix: Informational only; this passes with a note when TRIM is on, since it is the usual choice.
catalogue.why: Reveals which blocks are in use (not their contents). Usually an acceptable trade-off.

catalogue.title: Automatic login enabled
catalogue.fix: Disable autologin (root). Explain the keyring consequences before and after.
catalogue.why: Anyone who powers on the device (after LUKS unlock, if any) gets the full session. Usually also leads to a blank keyring password (auth.keyring_blank).

catalogue.title: User account has an empty password
catalogue.fix: Set a password with passwd.

catalogue.title: Screen lock disabled, delayed, or not applied on suspend
detect: GNOME: org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled, lock-delay; org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay (0 = never)
KDE: kreadconfig6 --file kscreenlockerrc --group Daemon --key Autolock / Timeout / LockOnResume (empty = default)
catalogue.fix: Enable locking, idle timeout of 5 minutes or less, lock on suspend and lid close.

modifiers.when_text: device type is desktop and not several user accounts

catalogue.verify: KDE defaults are not written to the file; treat a missing key as the default.

catalogue.title: Notification content shown on the lock screen
catalogue.fix: Disable notification previews on the lock screen.
catalogue.verify: Confirm the equivalent KDE/Cinnamon setting and key location per version.

catalogue.title: Keyring or wallet with a blank password (secrets stored unencrypted)
detect: GNOME Keyring: $XDG_DATA_HOME/keyrings/*.keyring; encrypted files begin with the binary magic "GnomeKeyring\n\r\0\n", unencrypted ones are plain-text INI starting with "[keyring]"
catalogue.fix: Set a keyring password via Seahorse or KWalletManager; explain the trade-off with autologin.
catalogue.why: Saved Wi-Fi, email, browser and app secrets are readable by anyone with file access.
catalogue.verify: Confirm a reliable way to detect a blank-password KWallet.

catalogue.title: Chromium/Electron apps using the "basic" password store
detect: Launch flags: --password-store=basic in ~/.config/*-flags.conf, .desktop Exec lines, wrapper scripts
Profile "Login Data" (SQLite) logins.password_value and "Cookies" encrypted_value: prefix "v10" = hardcoded key, "v11" = keyring key
Check that a Secret Service provider is on the session bus (org.freedesktop.secrets)
catalogue.fix: Ensure gnome-keyring or KWallet Secret Service is running; remove the flag; re-save credentials.
catalogue.why: Without a Secret Service keyring, saved passwords and cookies are encrypted with a hardcoded key, which is effectively plaintext.

catalogue.title: Remote desktop or screen sharing server enabled
detect: GNOME: grdctl status; systemctl --user is-active gnome-remote-desktop
KDE: krdpserver / krfb in autostart or running
systemctl is-active xrdp x11vnc; ss -tlnp for 3389 and 5900-5910
catalogue.fix: Disable when not needed; otherwise require strong credentials and bind to a VPN interface.

catalogue.title: SSH private keys without a passphrase
detect: For each private key in ~/.ssh: "ssh-keygen -y -P \"\" -f <key>" succeeds = no passphrase
catalogue.fix: ssh-keygen -p -f <key>; recommend an agent (ssh-agent, gnome-keyring, KeePassXC).

catalogue.title: Plaintext credential files
detect: .env files under home (limit depth, skip node_modules)
Also flag group/world-readable permissions on any of these
catalogue.fix: Move to credential helpers (git-credential-libsecret, docker credential helpers); chmod 600 at minimum.

catalogue.title: Shell and REPL history containing secrets
detect: Patterns: password=, passwd, -p<value>, token, secret, Authorization:, Bearer, AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}, ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}, xox[bp]-
catalogue.fix: Offer per-line redaction; suggest HISTCONTROL=ignorespace (bash) or setopt HIST_IGNORE_SPACE (zsh).

catalogue.title: Passwordless sudo
catalogue.fix: Remove NOPASSWD entries via visudo.
catalogue.why: Lets malware running as the user escalate silently.

catalogue.title: Firefox or Thunderbird without a Primary Password
detect: If logins.json is non-empty, use NSS on key4.db: PK11_NeedLogin on the internal key slot
catalogue.fix: Guide the user to set a Primary Password.
catalogue.verify: Firefox 157 on Linux Mint 22 keeps profiles in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mozilla/firefox (seen 2026-10-03); check other distributions and whether older ~/.mozilla profiles are moved there.

catalogue.title: Home directory readable by other users
detect: stat -c %a $HOME  (flag if the "other" digit is non-zero)
catalogue.fix: chmod 750 or 700 $HOME (warn about ~/public_html and similar).

catalogue.title: GPG secret keys without a passphrase
catalogue.fix: gpg --edit-key <id> passwd.

catalogue.title: New files can be read by other accounts (default umask)
detect: umask  (0022 = new files readable by other users)
catalogue.fix: Suggest 027 or 077 in the login profile.

catalogue.title: SSH known_hosts lists the servers you connect to
detect: ~/.ssh/known_hosts: lines whose first field does not start with "|1|" are plain host names
~/.ssh/config: HashKnownHosts yes (new entries are then hashed)
catalogue.fix: ssh-keygen -H -f ~/.ssh/known_hosts (the plain copy it leaves as known_hosts.old is deleted), and HashKnownHosts yes in ~/.ssh/config. The file is backed up for revert.
catalogue.why: ~/.ssh/known_hosts names every server this account has ever connected to. Hashed entries still verify servers but don't reveal them to whoever reads the file.

catalogue.title: Login history readable by every user
detect: stat /var/log/wtmp /var/log/lastlog /var/log/btmp (and wtmp.1, lastlog under /var/lib/wtmpdb): flag world-readable
catalogue.fix: chmod o-r on wtmp and lastlog (non-administrators then can't run `last`); btmp should already be root-only.
catalogue.why: /var/log/wtmp and /var/log/lastlog record when, and from which address, every account logged in; the `last` and `lastlog` commands show them to any user.

catalogue.title: Services listening on all interfaces
detect: Allowlist expected listeners (DHCP client on 68, mDNS on 5353 handled by net.hostname_broadcast)

Active firewall: ufw status verbose (root), or firewall-cmd --list-all for the active zones; a port the firewall blocks is listening but not reachable (firewall_blocks_exposed when all of them are). nftables/iptables rulesets are not interpreted: unknown.
catalogue.fix: Disable unneeded services, bind dev servers to 127.0.0.1, disable SSH password and root login.

modifiers.when_text: the firewall blocks the exposed services

catalogue.title: Docker published ports bypass the host firewall
catalogue.fix: Publish as 127.0.0.1:<port>:<port>, or add rules to the DOCKER-USER chain.
catalogue.why: Docker inserts its own iptables/nftables rules ahead of ufw (and often firewalld zones).

catalogue.title: Host firewall disabled
detect: ufw status; firewall-cmd --state; nft list ruleset (empty = no rules)
catalogue.fix: Enable ufw or firewalld with a default-deny inbound policy.

catalogue.title: Wi-Fi connections use the permanent MAC address
detect: NetworkManager --print-config [device] wifi.scan-rand-mac-address (default yes; no = the permanent address while scanning)
catalogue.fix: Set "stable" (stable per network) by default, "random" for hostile networks; note captive portal side effects.
catalogue.why: Lets public networks and their operators recognise the device across visits.

catalogue.title: Identifying hostname broadcast via DHCP and mDNS
detect: hostnamectl hostname; compare with the user's name from getent passwd (GECOS)
resolvectl status: a link with MulticastDNS=yes announces the hostname too (resolve only answers)
catalogue.fix: Offer a generic hostname, dhcp-send-hostname=no on untrusted networks, disable Avahi publishing if unused.

catalogue.title: KDE Connect / GSConnect enabled
catalogue.fix: Review paired devices and enabled plugins; disable when unused.
catalogue.why: Listens on the LAN and can sync notifications, clipboard and files with paired phones.

catalogue.title: VPN without DNS leak protection or kill switch
detect: While a VPN is up: resolvectl status; check non-VPN links do not provide DNS for the "~." routing domain
catalogue.fix: Configure DNS routing to the VPN link and a kill switch where the VPN client supports it.

catalogue.title: Unencrypted DNS
detect: resolvectl status (DNSOverTLS setting); check whether systemd-resolved is in use at all
catalogue.fix: Configure DNSOverTLS in resolved.conf.d with a chosen resolver, or use the browser's DoH.

catalogue.title: IPv6 privacy extensions disabled
detect: sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.use_tempaddr (and per interface); nmcli -g ipv6.ip6-privacy connection show <id>
catalogue.fix: Set use_tempaddr=2 / ip6-privacy=2.

catalogue.title: Saved hidden-SSID networks
catalogue.fix: Suggest making the network visible on the router, or removing the saved profile.
catalogue.why: The device broadcasts the network names in probe requests wherever it goes.

catalogue.title: Bluetooth always on, discoverable, or named after the user
catalogue.fix: Non-discoverable and a generic alias (recommended); turning the radio off is offered as a separate step, since it disconnects whatever is connected.

catalogue.title: Connectivity checks to distro servers
catalogue.fix: Informational; can be disabled at the cost of captive-portal detection.

catalogue.title: Saved Wi-Fi networks record where this machine has been
detect: nmcli -g connection.timestamp connection show <uuid> for each 802-11-wireless connection (counts and ages, never names)
catalogue.fix: Forget networks not used for months (nmcli connection delete); the app lists which ones in the guide.
catalogue.why: Every saved network keeps the time it was last used, so together they are a history of places; their passwords sit in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections, readable from a live USB when the disk isn't encrypted.

catalogue.title: Saved open Wi-Fi networks reconnect automatically
detect: nmcli: 802-11-wireless connections with no 802-11-wireless-security.key-mgmt and connection.autoconnect yes
catalogue.fix: connection.autoconnect no for each; they still connect when chosen by hand.
catalogue.why: A saved network without a password is matched by its name alone, so any hotspot with the same name (an attacker's) gets this machine to join it without asking.

catalogue.title: Crash reporters and usage surveys
detect: Ubuntu: systemctl is-enabled apport whoopsie; /etc/default/apport enabled=
KDE: DrKonqi asks before sending; User Feedback has its own check (tel.kde_feedback)
catalogue.fix: Disable or set to ask before sending.
catalogue.why: Crash reports can include memory contents and are uploaded to vendors.

catalogue.title: Location services enabled
catalogue.fix: Disable globally or review per-app access.
catalogue.why: GeoClue sends nearby Wi-Fi access points to an online lookup service.

catalogue.title: Browser telemetry and studies
detect: Firefox and Thunderbird prefs: datareporting.healthreport.uploadEnabled, toolkit.telemetry.enabled, app.shield.optoutstudies.enabled
Chromium family: MetricsReportingEnabled policy in /etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed, /etc/chromium/policies/managed, etc.
catalogue.fix: Apply enterprise policies (root) or per-profile prefs (user).

catalogue.title: Developer tool telemetry
detect: VS Code / VSCodium: settings.json "telemetry.telemetryLevel"; GitHub Copilot extension noted (sends code to GitHub)

Env vars: DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT, HOMEBREW_NO_ANALYTICS, NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, CHECKPOINT_DISABLE (HashiCorp), AZURE_CORE_COLLECT_TELEMETRY, SAM_CLI_TELEMETRY, GATSBY_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, NUXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, ASTRO_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, STRIPE_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT, DO_NOT_TRACK
catalogue.fix: Set opt-out env vars in ~/.config/environment.d/*.conf and the VS Code setting.
catalogue.verify: The JetBrains usage.statistics.xml layout, and which tools honour DO_NOT_TRACK.

catalogue.title: Package repositories over plain HTTP
catalogue.fix: Switch to HTTPS mirrors.
catalogue.why: Packages are signature-verified, but network observers can see what software is installed.

catalogue.title: Fedora counts this computer in its statistics (DNF countme)
catalogue.fix: Set countme=0 (anonymous weekly counter; informational).

catalogue.title: KDE user feedback (telemetry) enabled
detect: ~/.config/PlasmaUserFeedback [Global] FeedbackLevel: absent or 0 = disabled (KUserFeedback NoTelemetry); 16 basic system information, 32, 48, 64 send more each
catalogue.fix: FeedbackLevel=0 (kwriteconfig, reversible).
catalogue.why: Plasma can send system and usage statistics to KDE; it is off unless turned on.

catalogue.title: Accounts and sync clients that copy data off this machine
detect: Nextcloud, ownCloud, Dropbox, Insync, MEGA, OneDrive clients: their config directories, native and Flatpak
catalogue.fix: Informational; review what each account and client syncs, and whether it is end-to-end encrypted.
catalogue.why: Not a fault: an inventory of what leaves this machine by design, so it can be weighed with the rest. Online accounts sync calendars, contacts and mail; sync clients copy folders.

catalogue.title: Services that contact servers in the background
detect: systemctl is-enabled fwupd-refresh.timer; snapd.service active; packagekit-background.timer / PackageKit
systemd-timesyncd or chronyd: configured NTP servers (timesyncd.conf, chrony.conf), else the distribution pool
catalogue.fix: Informational; each can be turned off at a cost (no firmware updates, no snap updates, drifting clock).
catalogue.why: Not telemetry, but regular contact that shows the machine's address to someone: firmware metadata from LVFS, Snap Store refresh checks, package metadata, and time servers.

catalogue.title: Chromium-family crash dumps on disk
detect: <profile root>/Crash Reports/{pending,completed}, for google-chrome, chromium, BraveSoftware/Brave-Browser, microsoft-edge, vivaldi
catalogue.fix: Delete existing dumps; disable crash/metrics reporting by policy.
catalogue.why: Minidumps can contain memory fragments, including URLs and content from incognito windows.
catalogue.verify: Measure (fatrace, iotop) whether dumps are written locally when reporting is disabled, and how much the browser writes overall, before the app makes any claim about SSD wear.

catalogue.title: Extensions with access to all sites
detect: Chromium: <profile>/Extensions/<id>/<version>/manifest.json permissions and host_permissions containing <all_urls>, *://*/*, http://*/*, https://*/*
catalogue.fix: List them with names and let the user review or remove.

catalogue.title: History, cookies and site data kept indefinitely
detect: Firefox: privacy.sanitize.sanitizeOnShutdown and related clearOnShutdown prefs
catalogue.fix: Offer clear-on-exit for cookies, cache and history, with exceptions for sites the user wants to stay logged in to.

catalogue.title: Weak tracking protection
detect: Chromium: BlockThirdPartyCookies policy (default allows third-party cookies)
catalogue.fix: Strict mode in Firefox; block third-party cookies in Chromium.

catalogue.title: Private-session downloads leaking through the OS
detect: Cross-reference files in the Downloads directory with desk.thumbnails, desk.recent_files and desk.indexers
catalogue.fix: Point to the related clean-ups.
catalogue.why: The browser forgets them, but thumbnails, recent-file lists and indexers still record them.

catalogue.title: Disk cache and session store on persistent storage
catalogue.fix: Memory-only cache, sessionstore privacy level 2, or profile-sync-daemon.

catalogue.title: WebRTC IP exposure
catalogue.fix: Restrict to the default route; mostly relevant with split-tunnel VPNs.

catalogue.title: Browser signed in to an account that syncs history and passwords
detect: Chromium: <profile>/Preferences account_info non-empty or sync.has_setup_completed; sync.encryption passphrase flags
Firefox: services.sync.username in prefs.js (only whether it is set, never the address)
catalogue.fix: Sign out, or sync fewer data types; in Chrome set a sync passphrase so Google can't read it.
catalogue.why: With sync on, history, passwords, bookmarks and open tabs are copied to Google, Microsoft or Mozilla. Firefox Sync is end-to-end encrypted; Chrome and Edge sync can be read by the provider unless a sync passphrase is set.
catalogue.verify: The Preferences keys for a custom sync passphrase across Chrome versions.

catalogue.title: Browser ad and suggestion features that report what you do
detect: Chromium: Preferences privacy_sandbox.m1.topics_enabled / fledge_enabled / ad_measurement_enabled, search.suggest_enabled, safebrowsing.enhanced
catalogue.fix: Firefox prefs while it is closed; Chromium policies (PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled, PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled, PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled, SearchSuggestEnabled) for every user, or the settings page per profile.
catalogue.why: Chrome's Privacy Sandbox profiles your interests for advertisers from your history; search suggestions send every keystroke in the address bar to the search engine; sponsored shortcuts and suggestions in Firefox report what is shown and clicked.
catalogue.verify: Chromium's Preferences keys for the Privacy Sandbox APIs, and the policy names, on current releases.

catalogue.title: Thumbnail cache persists and references sensitive locations
detect: Parse PNG tEXt chunk Thumb::URI; flag orphans (file no longer exists)
Flag URIs under /media, /run/media, VeraCrypt mount points, or other crypt mounts separate from home
App-specific caches: gThumb, Shotwell, digiKam (see app.photo_dbs)
catalogue.fix: Delete orphans and sensitive entries; set a maximum age; optionally keep the cache in memory: a tmpfs line in /etc/fstab for $XDG_CACHE_HOME/thumbnails (size-capped, nofail), mounted at once, so it is empty at every boot.

modifiers.when_text: thumbnails show files from removable or encrypted drives

catalogue.why: Thumbnails survive deletion of the original, and each PNG embeds Thumb::URI (the full original path). Browsing an open encrypted container or USB stick leaves images and paths outside it.

catalogue.title: Recent files list (recently-used.xbel)
catalogue.fix: Clear; disable or set a short maximum age.
catalogue.why: Written by any GTK app regardless of desktop, so KDE users have it too.

catalogue.title: KDE activity database and recent documents
detect: Plasma 6 per-app state in $XDG_STATE_HOME/*staterc (Dolphin, Kate, etc.)
catalogue.fix: Stop kactivitymanagerd, clear the event and score tables, clear RecentDocuments, apply settings, restart.
catalogue.why: Users report that the activity database keeps recording even when history is turned off.
catalogue.verify: Confirm table names and pluginsrc key names on the target Plasma version.

catalogue.title: File content indexers (Baloo, LocalSearch/Tracker)
detect: GNOME 47+: localsearch status; older: tracker3 status; data in $XDG_CACHE_HOME/tracker3
catalogue.fix: Basic (filename-only) indexing or disable; exclude sensitive folders and mount points; purge the index.
catalogue.why: Indexers extract text from documents into their own database, which can retain content after deletion and can cover mounted encrypted containers.

catalogue.title: Clipboard history saved to disk
detect: Klipper: $XDG_DATA_HOME/klipper/ and klipperrc (save history across sessions)
GNOME extensions (e.g. Clipboard Indicator): check the extension's cache directory
catalogue.fix: Clear; disable persistence; recommend password managers that set the clipboard-exclusion hint and auto-clear.
catalogue.why: Copied passwords and sensitive text persist across reboots.
catalogue.verify: Klipper storage format changed in Plasma 6; confirm file names.

catalogue.title: Zeitgeist activity log
catalogue.fix: Clear and disable.

catalogue.title: File manager and viewers keep notes on each file (GVFS metadata)
catalogue.fix: Stop gvfsd-metadata and clear.

catalogue.title: Screenshots accumulating automatically
catalogue.fix: Report count and age; offer review.

catalogue.title: GNOME application usage tracking
catalogue.fix: Disable and clear.

catalogue.title: Session restore reopens apps and documents
catalogue.fix: Start with an empty session.

catalogue.title: File manager per-folder view records
catalogue.fix: Informational; offer cleanup.

catalogue.title: Photo manager databases, including face recognition data
detect: digiKam: digikam4.db, thumbnails-digikam.db, recognition.db (in the collection root by default)
gThumb: native and Flatpak (org.gnome.gThumb) cache directories
catalogue.fix: Inform; offer to clear caches and face data.

catalogue.title: Messenger and email local stores
detect: Signal ~/.config/Signal; Telegram $XDG_DATA_HOME/TelegramDesktop; Discord ~/.config/discord; Slack ~/.config/Slack; Thunderbird profiles
catalogue.fix: Recommend local passcodes (Telegram), keyring-backed safeStorage, attachment cache cleanup.

catalogue.title: Editor swap, backup and undo files
detect: Vim: ~/.viminfo, swap files (.*.swp next to files or in directory option), undodir
gedit: file~ backups; Kate: swap file directory (configurable)
catalogue.fix: Offer cleanup; suggest swap/undo directories on tmpfs or inside the encrypted container.
catalogue.why: Copies of files edited inside encrypted containers can end up outside them.

catalogue.title: Office suite recent lists and autorecovery copies
catalogue.fix: Clear history via the app (editing registrymodifications.xcu directly is fragile); clear backup copies.

catalogue.title: Media player history and resume data
catalogue.fix: Clear; disable recent lists where supported.

catalogue.title: Print jobs and history retained by CUPS
catalogue.fix: Set PreserveJobFiles No and PreserveJobHistory to No or a short time; purge completed jobs.
catalogue.why: By default CUPS keeps document files for a day and job history (including titles) indefinitely.

catalogue.title: PDF reader document history
catalogue.fix: Clear.

catalogue.title: Electron app caches
catalogue.fix: Clear only while the app is not running.

catalogue.title: Package manager logs reveal installation history
catalogue.fix: Informational.

catalogue.title: Mail clients load remote content (tracking pixels)
detect: Evolution: gsettings org.gnome.evolution.mail image-loading-policy (never | sometimes | always)
catalogue.fix: Thunderbird pref back to blocked (while it is closed); Evolution image-loading-policy never.
catalogue.why: Loading images from the sender's server tells them when, where and on what you opened a message. Both clients block it by default; this catches it turned on.

catalogue.title: Documents you save carry your name
detect: LibreOffice registrymodifications.xcu: /org.openoffice.UserProfile/Data givenname or sn set (whether, not what)
mat2 / exiftool installed, for stripping metadata from files by hand
catalogue.fix: Turn on "Remove personal information on saving" (while LibreOffice is closed); recommend mat2 for photos.
catalogue.why: LibreOffice writes the user name from its settings into every document's author and editing history, and photos can carry GPS coordinates; both travel with the file when shared.
catalogue.verify: The registrymodifications.xcu paths for RemovePersonalInfoOnSaving on LibreOffice 7 and 24.x.

catalogue.title: Flatpak apps with broad permissions
detect: flatpak list --app --columns=application; flatpak info --show-permissions <id>; flatpak override --show <id>
Flag filesystems=home|host|host-os|host-etc, devices=all, session bus access
Flag talk access to org.freedesktop.Flatpak as critical (allows escaping the sandbox)
catalogue.fix: flatpak override --user --nofilesystem=home <id> (and similar); suggest Flatseal.

catalogue.title: Flatpak apps keep separate caches and history
catalogue.fix: Every other check must enumerate these paths; this check reports totals.
catalogue.why: Cleaners that only look at native paths miss everything under ~/.var/app.

catalogue.title: X11 session allows apps to snoop on each other
catalogue.fix: Recommend a Wayland session where the hardware and apps allow it.
catalogue.why: Any X11 client can log keystrokes and capture other windows, including password prompts.

catalogue.title: Leftover data from uninstalled apps
detect: Native ~/.config and ~/.local/share dirs with no matching installed package (low confidence)
catalogue.fix: List for review; never auto-delete native candidates.

catalogue.title: Persisted portal permissions (camera, microphone, location, screenshots)
catalogue.fix: Review; flatpak permission-reset <id>.

catalogue.title: Snap retained revisions and classic confinement
detect: snap list --all (disabled revisions); snap get system refresh.retain
catalogue.fix: Remove disabled revisions; inform about classic snaps.

catalogue.title: AppImages run without a sandbox
catalogue.fix: Informational; prefer the Flatpak where the app offers one, and keep AppImages from sources you trust.
catalogue.why: An AppImage is a plain program with full access to your files; nothing confines it.

catalogue.title: Security updates not applied
catalogue.fix: Prompt to update; offer automatic security updates where the distro supports them.

catalogue.title: Processes can read each other's memory (ptrace_scope 0)
catalogue.fix: sysctl.d drop-in kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1 (note it affects attaching debuggers).
catalogue.why: Any process running as the user can read password manager and browser memory.

catalogue.title: Any user can read the kernel log (dmesg_restrict 0)
detect: Members of adm / systemd-journal can still read kernel messages through the journal
catalogue.fix: sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 now and a sysctl.d drop-in for boot (root, reversible).
catalogue.why: The kernel log records every USB device plugged in (with serial numbers), drives mounted, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth activity: a record of what was done with the machine, readable by every account and every program.

catalogue.title: Other users can see your processes and their command lines
detect: /proc/self/mountinfo: options of the /proc mount; hidepid=2 or hidepid=invisible (or 1/noaccess) hides them
catalogue.fix: Explain the fstab option (hidepid=invisible,gid=proc) and that systemd-logind, polkit and monitoring tools need the gid exception; some distributions break without it. Never automate.
catalogue.why: Without hidepid on /proc, every account can list what you run with its full command line, including passwords and tokens passed as arguments.
catalogue.verify: Which distributions' logind and polkit work with hidepid out of the box.

catalogue.title: Freed memory isn't cleared (init_on_free)
catalogue.fix: Explain the kernel parameter and its performance cost.
catalogue.why: Freed memory keeps its old contents until it is reused, so secrets linger a little longer for a memory dump or cold-boot attack to find. Defence in depth with a real performance cost, which is why few distributions enable it; live data is in memory either way, so it narrows the risk rather than removing it.

catalogue.title: Kernel can't keep sandboxed programs from the session's hidden sockets (Landlock)
catalogue.fix: A kernel 6.12 or newer.
catalogue.why: Landlock.

catalogue.title: Kernel memory isn't cleared before use (init_on_alloc)
catalogue.fix: Explain the kernel parameter and its performance cost.
catalogue.why: Kernel hardening against bugs that leak uninitialised kernel memory to programs. Not a serious threat on its own, but it is on by default in almost every distribution kernel, costs almost nothing and meaningfully improves security, so finding it off is strange: it usually means a custom kernel or a boot option turned it off, and is worth looking into.

catalogue.title: Suspend keeps disk keys in RAM
detect: Memory encryption: /proc/cpuinfo flags sme (AMD; active with mem_encrypt=on or CONFIG_AMD_MEM_ENCRYPT_ACTIVE_BY_DEFAULT) or tme (Intel; turned on in firmware, the kernel log says "x86/tme: enabled by BIOS")
catalogue.fix: Advise shutting down when travelling; note memory encryption when the CPU has it but it is off.
catalogue.why: A stolen sleeping laptop has its keys in memory, exposed to DMA or cold-boot attacks.

catalogue.title: Thunderbolt/DMA protections weak
catalogue.fix: Explain enabling IOMMU and bolt security levels. Note that memory encryption (SME/TME) is no substitute.

catalogue.title: Phone-home traffic seen on the network
detect: With root: resolvectl monitor --json=short (DNS names asked) and ss -tunp samples (which program) for N seconds
Without root: ss -tunp samples of your own programs, matched against addresses of known phone-home hosts
Match names against a list of known telemetry, crash-report, connectivity-check and location hosts
Other names are only counted per program, never listed: they would be your browsing
catalogue.fix: Point to the check that turns off what was seen (browser telemetry, crash reporters, connectivity check...).
catalogue.why: Settings say what should happen; watching the traffic shows what does. Confirms that telemetry, crash reporting and connectivity checks you turned off really stopped.
catalogue.verify: The host list, and resolvectl monitor's JSON format (systemd 254+).
contacts: Nobody: it only watches. Without root it looks up the addresses of known phone-home hosts (your DNS resolver sees those lookups).

catalogue.title: DNS over TLS configured but not used
detect: Only when resolved has DNSOverTLS set
resolvectl query --cache=no <probe name>: "Data was acquired via local or encrypted transport: yes|no"
catalogue.fix: Use DNSOverTLS=yes with a server that supports it (see net.dns_unencrypted's guide).
catalogue.why: systemd-resolved can be set to DNS over TLS yet fall back to plain DNS (opportunistic mode, or a server that doesn't support it) without saying so.
catalogue.verify: The resolvectl query output line across systemd versions.
contacts: Your configured DNS server: one lookup of example.com.

catalogue.title: DNS queries leak outside the VPN
detect: Get a test id from the leak-test service, look up unique names under it, ask the service which resolvers asked
With a VPN: resolvers run by a different network than the VPN exit may be leaking
Without a VPN: informational, shows who resolves your names
catalogue.fix: Use the VPN's DNS (its app's DNS leak protection), or route all DNS through the tunnel (resolved ~. on the VPN link).
catalogue.why: With a VPN on, the sites you look up should be resolved through it. If queries reach your internet provider's resolvers instead, it sees every site you visit despite the VPN.
catalogue.verify: The bash.ws API and JSON format.
contacts: bash.ws (the leak-test service): sees your public IP address and which resolvers asked for its test names.
Your DNS resolvers: ten lookups of random names under bash.ws.

catalogue.title: DNS answers aren't checked with DNSSEC
detect: Look up a correctly signed name (it must resolve) and dnssec-failed.org (deliberately broken: must fail)
catalogue.fix: Explain resolved's DNSSEC= setting and validating resolvers; many networks break DNSSEC, so allow-downgrade is common.
catalogue.why: Without DNSSEC validation, a forged DNS answer (on public Wi-Fi, or from a compromised resolver) is accepted and can send you to the wrong server.
contacts: Your DNS resolver: lookups of example.com and dnssec-failed.org (its servers see the second lookup).

catalogue.title: Failed DNS lookups are redirected
detect: Look up a random, non-existent .com name; any address in reply means NXDOMAIN rewriting
catalogue.fix: Use a different DNS resolver (or DNS over TLS), and turn off "DNS assist" / "search help" in the provider account or router.
catalogue.why: Some providers and routers answer lookups of names that don't exist with their own server (for search pages or ads): they are reading and altering your DNS.
contacts: Your DNS resolver: one lookup of a random, non-existent .com name (the .com servers see it too).

catalogue.title: IPv6 traffic bypasses the VPN
detect: IPv6 default route via a non-VPN interface
Ask an IPv6 address echo service which address it sees; a global address of a non-VPN interface is a leak
Also show the public IPv4 address websites see
catalogue.fix: Turn on the VPN's IPv6 support or leak protection, or disable IPv6 on the physical interface while the VPN is on.
catalogue.why: Many VPN setups only carry IPv4. If IPv6 still works outside the tunnel, sites reachable over IPv6 see your real address.
contacts: api.ipify.org and api6.ipify.org (address echo services): see your public IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

catalogue.title: The router forwards internet ports to this machine (UPnP)
detect: SSDP search for an Internet Gateway Device on the local network
Its description, then GetGenericPortMappingEntry for each mapping; keep those whose internal client is this machine
catalogue.fix: Turn off UPnP in the app that opened the port, or in the router. Then check the service with net.exposed_services.
catalogue.why: Apps (games, torrent clients, media servers) can ask the router to open ports to them with UPnP, without asking you. Those services are then reachable from the whole internet.
contacts: Your router only (local network): an SSDP search and its UPnP control interface. Nothing on the internet.

catalogue.title: Encrypted connections are intercepted
detect: TLS connections to a few well-known sites; who issued their certificates
An issuer known for interception (antivirus, corporate proxies, debugging proxies) fails; an unknown issuer or an untrusted certificate warns
Also note root certificates added locally (/usr/local/share/ca-certificates, /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors, ...)
catalogue.fix: Find the product doing it (the issuer names it) and turn off its HTTPS scanning, or remove its root certificate.
catalogue.why: A corporate proxy, antivirus "web shield" or network device that decrypts HTTPS sees passwords, messages and everything else sent to websites.
catalogue.verify: The lists of public and intercepting issuers.
contacts: www.wikipedia.org, www.mozilla.org, letsencrypt.org, www.debian.org: a TLS connection to each (they see your IP address).

catalogue.title: Security updates not applied (with fresh package lists)
detect: apt: apt-get update into a temporary lists directory as you (the system lists are not touched), then apt list --upgradable
dnf: dnf check-update --refresh (and updateinfo --security); pacman: checkupdates; flatpak remote-ls --updates; snap refresh --list
catalogue.fix: Install the updates (see kern.updates).
catalogue.why: The offline check counts only updates the machine already knows about; this one fetches fresh package lists first, so it also counts what was published since your last refresh.
catalogue.verify: apt-get update as a normal user into its own lists directory.
contacts: Your distribution's package mirrors (as in its repository files), Flathub and the Snap Store if used: they see your IP address. apt downloads tens of MB of lists.

catalogue.title: Services reachable from the internet over IPv6
detect: Listening services on all interfaces that the host firewall lets through
With a port probe server of your own (online.json port_probe): ask it to connect to each one from outside
Otherwise: likely reachable; confirm with daprivacyscanner --probe from a device on another network
catalogue.fix: Stop the service, bind it to a local address, or block it in the host firewall (see net.exposed_services).
catalogue.why: With a public IPv6 address there is no home-router NAT in the way: a listening service the host firewall lets through can be reached from anywhere, unless the router blocks it.
contacts: Nobody by default. With a port probe server set: that server, which connects to your public IPv6 address on the listed ports.

reads.why: To tell which filesystems and swap are encrypted and where a hibernation image would go.
reads.how: lsblk, /proc/swaps, /proc/mounts, /sys/power, /etc/crypttab; LUKS headers only with administrator access, through the helper (versions and key-slot types, never keys or salts).

reads.why: Automatic login, screen lock, notifications on the lock screen.
reads.how: Display manager files under /etc, gsettings, KDE's kscreenlockerrc; /etc/shadow only with administrator access, and only whether an account's password field is empty.

reads.why: To find secrets stored without a passphrase or in plain text.
reads.how: The first bytes of ~/.ssh keys, keyring and GnuPG files (to see whether they are encrypted); whether ~/.netrc, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.git-credentials, ~/.docker/config.json and similar hold a credential. Their contents never appear in the report: only that they do, and their permissions.

reads.why: To count lines that look like passwords or tokens.
reads.how: ~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history, fish, Python, psql and MySQL histories. The report holds counts, never the lines.

reads.why: Telemetry, tracking protection, history retention, extensions, sync, crash dumps.
reads.how: prefs.js, Preferences, Local State and extension manifests of Firefox-family and Chromium-family profiles; Login Data and Cookies are opened read-only to count entries encrypted with the built-in key. No URLs, cookies or passwords are read into the report.

reads.why: Thumbnails, recent files, KDE activity and clipboard histories.
reads.how: The thumbnail cache (each PNG's embedded path, to see which drive it came from), recently-used.xbel, kactivitymanagerd's database (counts), clipboard managers' folders (sizes).

reads.why: Caches, histories and backups that outlive the files they came from.
reads.how: Sizes and counts under ~/.config, ~/.local/share, ~/.cache, ~/.var/app and ~/snap; LibreOffice, media players, PDF readers, editors, messengers and mail clients.

reads.why: Exposed services, firewall, DNS, Wi-Fi settings, Bluetooth, VPN.
reads.how: ss, nmcli (saved connections' settings and last-used times, never passwords), resolvectl, bluetoothctl, /proc/net; ufw's rules only with administrator access.

reads.why: Crash reporting, journal retention, updates, kernel hardening, sandboxing.
reads.how: systemd and apt/dnf settings under /etc, /proc/sys, package lists already on disk (nothing is downloaded), flatpak and snap listings.

reads.why: To skip apps that are running when a fix would clear their data, and to spot guest agents, indexers and remote desktop servers.
reads.how: Process names from /proc, and which of your own processes hold a file open under a folder a fix would clear.

never: Nothing is sent anywhere during a scan. The online tests are separate, run only when you start them, and each says who it contacts first.
File contents are never copied into the report: it holds paths, counts and settings.
Scans change nothing. Fixes show exactly what they will do first, and settings changes can be reverted from History.
